title: Prosecutor alleges Tata Steel intentionally polluted IJmuiden 598 times
intro: Tata Steel's Dutch operations lead today's edition. NL Times reports that a prosecutor has alleged the company intentionally polluted at its IJmuiden site 598 times. Separately, UA.NEWS, citing Anadolu Agency, reports that a criminal case against Tata Steel has begun in Amsterdam. Labour relations also feature prominently. U.S. Steel has a tentative four-year deal with steelworkers, steelworkers at four Cleveland-Cliffs mines have ratified a contract and POSCO has reached a revised tentative wage deal. In China, Yieh Corp. reports that industry profits fell 27.4% in Q1-Q3 on weak demand and overcapacity. Trade measures continue to multiply, from British melt-country reporting to OECD findings on Latin American imports. Much of today's material consists of headlines alone, and we note the gaps where they arise.

marketOverview: Today's material contains little hard price data. Shanghai Metals Market (SMM) says macro and fundamental factors are jointly pushing iron ore lower, but it expects the decline to slow and stabilise next week. Wisevoter reports that Chinese coking coal futures have hit a three-month low. A separate SMM analysis headline says steel billet has peaked. In Vietnam, three companies raised selling prices, with the highest increase reaching 200,000 VND per ton, according to Vietnam.vn. kalkine.ca argues that steel prices face a demand test. None of the excerpts give benchmark price levels for iron ore, coal, billet or finished steel, so readers should take direction rather than magnitude from today's reports.

analysis: Analysis: two threads run through today's material. First, trade defence appears to be becoming more granular. The UK's melt-country reporting requirement, as reported by Metallurgprom, could make it harder to route steel through third countries to avoid trade measures. The OECD's findings on Latin America, with imports up 47% and utilisation at 60%, suggest pressure on regions with weaker protection. If Chinese profitability stays weak, as the 27.4% decline reported by Yieh Corp. indicates, exporters may continue to look abroad, which would likely sustain this policy response. Second, labour settlements in the US and South Korea could reduce the near-term risk of disruption. However, the terms are unknown, so their cost implications cannot be assessed from the material. For Tata Steel, the Dutch proceedings could weigh on the company's standing in the Netherlands, but the excerpts give neither its response nor any potential penalties. Meanwhile, Germany's procurement budget and Stegra's installation progress suggest that green steel is moving from plans towards physical assets and committed buyers. On the evidence here, the scale is still modest.
